( i ) Logical readiness indicates whether a request is eligible to proceed . ( ii ) State readiness characterizes the work required to make a request’s KV state available for GPU execution. ( iii ) Execution readiness characterizes whether a request selected by state admission can be efficiently integrated into the current model iteration. Coda bridges the gaps between these readiness views through controlled admission. 4.1 Admission Model We define three readiness views applied in sequence along the path from request availability to GPU execution: • Logical readiness. Logical readiness characterizes whether a request is eligible to proceed . A request becomes logically ready when ( i ) a user submits a new request or ( ii ) a tool call returns and the agent session can continue. • State readiness. State readiness characterizes the work required to make a request’s KV state available in GPU HBM. The three cases follow the storage hierarchy from highest to lowest readiness: ( i ) the KV state is resident in HBM and immediately usable; ( ii ) reusable KV state resides in CPU DRAM and requires restoration; or ( iii ) reusable KV state exists only on SSD and must be loaded, or no reusable copy exists and the prefix must be recomputed. • Execution readiness. Execution readiness characterizes the context-length compatibility between a state-selected request and the current participating requests . It distinguishes two conditions: ( i ) the request is compatible with the active context composition and can execute efficiently with the existing population; or ( ii ) the request introduces substantial context heterogeneity, requiring the resulting population to be reorganized for efficient model execution. Together, these views define the admission path: the admission layer uses logical readiness to form the candidate set, state readiness to select which request is prepared next , and execution readiness to organize the participating requests for efficient attention execution . Figure 6 illustrates this three-stage admission path. Figure 6 : Illustration of the three readiness stages in a request’s lifecycle. Logical readiness indicates that a request is available after a user request arrives or a tool call returns. State readiness characterizes the work required to make its KV state available in GPU HBM, including tier restoration, recomputation, and incremental-input prefill. Execution readiness indicates whether the request can execute efficiently with the currently active requests: compatible contexts execute as one complete batch, while heterogeneous contexts are organized into compatible cohorts (detailed in § 4.3 ). Dynamic readiness. Readiness evolves rapidly in coding-agent serving. User requests and asynchronous tool returns continuously change the logically ready population; long-lived session KV states grow and move across storage tiers; and resumed sessions repeatedly reshape the active context composition ( Findings 1-5 ). Consequently, state and execution readiness may change after a request first becomes logically ready. Coda reevaluates these views at their corresponding decision opportunities rather than fixing them at request arrival. Admission decisions. To bridge these dynamically changing readiness views , the admission layer makes two decisions: ( i ) State admission determines which logically ready request has its KV state prepared next according to its state readiness. ( ii ) Execution admission determines how the participating requests are organized for attention execution according to their execution readiness. The following subsections describe Tiered-Aging state admission (§ 4.2 ) and Compatibility-Aware execution admission (§ 4.3 ). 4.2 Tiered-Aging State Admission Admission challenge. State admission selects which logically ready request has its KV state prepared next . Long-lived coding-agent sessions accumulate large reusable prefixes that may move across storage tiers during tool-induced idle periods, while asynchronous tool returns continuously reshape the ready population. Consequently, newly ready requests incur substantially different computational costs for state preparation ( Findings 1-4 ). Coda uses Tiered-Aging state admission to exploit these differences while preserving progress. Tier-aware computational cost of state preparation. As described in § 4.1 , the current placement of a request’s KV state determines the work required before GPU execution. A coding-agent continuation contains a persistent session prefix and an incremental suffix introduced by a user request or tool return. The reusable prefix may be distributed across storage tiers, while the incremental suffix requires prefill computation. Dynamic reevaluation. User-request arrivals and tool completions immediately introduce new candidates, while tier movement during tool-induced idle periods changes their state computational costs. Tier-aware computational cost therefore captures where a persistent session’s KV state resides when the session resumes, while age captures how long the continuation has waited after becoming logically ready. Once the required KV state becomes available in HBM, the request proceeds to execution admission. State admission therefore determines which request is prepared next, while execution admission determines how the participating requests execute . 4.3 Compatibility-Aware Execution Admission Admission challenge. Execution admission determines how the requests participating in a model iteration are organized for attention execution . The contexts of long-lived coding-agent sessions grow at different rates, while the sessions resume asynchronously after tool calls. Consequently, requests with substantially different materialized context lengths frequently execute together, reducing decode efficiency ( Findings 4-7 ). Coda therefore uses Compatibility-Aware execution admission to select an efficient execution plan based on the current context composition. Context-length view.
